summary: This experimental document specifies a point-to-point route discovery mechanism that complements the core Routing Protocol for Low-power and Lossy Networks (RPL). It lets an IPv6 router discover routes on demand to other routers in a low-power and lossy network, meeting specified metric constraints.

plainLanguage.summary: Low-power sensor networks normally build one tree with a router at the top, and any two routers that want to talk must go through it. That is wasteful when they are near each other. RFC 6997 lets a router ask for a direct route to another router when it needs one, and to say how good the route has to be.

questions: on-demand routes in low-power lossy networks
how does rpl point-to-point route discovery work
subtitle: How a router in a low-power wireless network can find a route to another router on demand.

tldr.problem: In core RPL, two routers that are not the root can only talk along links of the DAG, so routes must be set up ahead of time and may be long and congest the root.
tldr.mechanism: The Origin builds a short-lived DAG rooted at itself using DIO messages in a new P2P Route Discovery mode. Each DIO accumulates a route, and the Target sends the chosen route back in a P2P-DRO message.
tldr.outcome: The discovered routes are guaranteed to meet the stated metric constraints but may not be the best. The RFC is Experimental, and the authors expected a later revision.

facts.label: Routes per Target
facts.value: 1 hop-by-hop or up to 4 source routes

today: RFC 6997 is an Experimental document that has not been obsoleted or updated. The document says it is presented as an Experimental specification to facilitate deployment in scenarios where reactive point-to-point route discovery is useful or necessary, and that it is anticipated that, once enough operational experience has been gained, the specification will be revised to progress towards the Standards Track. It asks for experience reports on secure operation, the rules for Trickle operation, the default configuration values, the policy for reusing instance identifiers, and the complexity of allowing several Target addresses in one discovery.

sections.title: Why On-Demand Point-to-Point Routes
sections.content:
For low-power and lossy networks, RPL provides paths along a directed acyclic graph rooted at a single router. Routers build and maintain the graph using destination-oriented DAG information object messages. When two arbitrary routers, neither of which is the root, need to communicate, the data packets are restricted to travel only along the links in the graph. That is not enough for several home automation and building automation applications, for two reasons.

The first is the need to pre-establish routes: each potential destination has to declare itself as such ahead of the time a source needs to reach it. The second is the need to route only along the links in the graph. A graph is built to optimise the routing cost to reach the root, so restricting point-to-point routes to its links may give significantly suboptimal routes and cause severe traffic congestion near the root.

The document describes an extension to core RPL that lets an IPv6 router discover routes to one or more other routers on demand. The discovered routes may not be the best available, but they are guaranteed to meet the specified routing metric constraints, so from the application's point of view they are good enough. This reactive discovery mechanism is called P2P-RPL.
sections.plainLanguage: Sensor networks are built as a tree with one gateway at the top, and two nearby sensors have to send everything through it. This proposal lets a sensor ask for a direct path when it needs one, instead of planning every path in advance.

sections.title: How a Route Discovery Works
sections.content:
A P2P-RPL route discovery takes place by forming a DAG rooted at the Origin. As in core RPL, the discovery uses IPv6 link-local multicast DIO messages to establish the graph, but unlike core RPL this graph is temporary. The routes are discovered and installed while it is alive; once the specified duration of their membership is over the routers leave and the graph ceases to exist. The installed routes are retained for their own specified lifetime, which is different from the duration of a router's membership in the graph.

Each router joining the graph determines a rank for itself and ignores subsequent DIOs from lower-ranked neighbours, so the discovery messages propagate away from the Origin rather than returning to it. As in core RPL, DIO generation is controlled by a Trickle timer, and P2P-RPL reuses the routing metrics, objective functions and packet-forwarding framework of core RPL.

The Origin may discover routes to one or more Targets identified by unicast or multicast addresses. It may find one hop-by-hop route or up to four source routes per Target. The DIOs that create the temporary graph are identified by a new mode of operation, P2P Route Discovery mode, and are called P2P mode DIOs. Each one carries exactly one P2P Route Discovery Option, in which the Origin states the address of a Target, whether it wants hop-by-hop or source routes, how many routes it wants when source routes are being discovered, and whether the Target should send a reply back when it receives the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The discovery works by growing a short-lived tree out from the router that needs the route. Every router on the way adds its own address to a list carried in the message, so by the time the message reaches the target, the list is the route. The tree then disappears again.

sections.title: The Route Discovery Option and Reply Message
sections.content:
The P2P Route Discovery Option, with option type 0x0a, is carried by both the P2P mode DIO and the reply message, and both must carry exactly one. Its fields carry the address of the Target, a flag asking for a reply, a flag choosing between hop-by-hop and source routes, the number of routes wanted, a count of the prefix octets elided from the addresses, the lifetime of a router's membership of the temporary graph, and a limit on the rank a router may hold. The option also holds a vector of IPv6 addresses representing the route accumulated so far in the forward direction, starting with the router next to the Origin. The Origin and Target addresses must not be in the vector, the vector must not contain any multicast address, and a router adding its address must ensure none of its addresses are already in it.

The lifetime field has four values: 0x00 means 1 second, 0x01 means 4 seconds, 0x02 means 16 seconds and 0x03 means 64 seconds. A router must leave the temporary graph once that time has passed since it joined.

The reply, the P2P Discovery Reply Object, carries a discovered source route back to the Origin, or establishes a hop-by-hop route as it travels back. It must carry exactly one route discovery option whose address vector holds the complete route, and it travels by link-local multicast along the route named in that vector. Its own fields include a Stop flag, which tells the routers that the discovery is over so that they generate no further DIOs, and an Ack Required flag, which asks the Origin to acknowledge receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: The route itself is carried as a list of addresses inside the messages. The reply travels back along that same list, and it can also carry a flag saying that the search is over so that the other routers stop sending discovery messages.

sections.title: Joining the Temporary DAG
sections.content:
All the routers taking part in a discovery, including the Origin and the Targets, must join the temporary graph. When a router joins one advertised by a P2P mode DIO, it must maintain its membership for the duration given by the lifetime field. The only purpose of the temporary graph is to carry out the discovery, and it must not be used to route data packets: joining it does not let a router install routing table entries that list its parents as next hops.

Because of that, the document disallows the solicitation of P2P mode DIOs with DODAG Information Solicitation messages, and a router taking part must not reset its Trickle timer or send a P2P mode DIO in response to a unicast solicitation. A router must detach from the temporary graph once its membership duration has elapsed, and after receiving a reply with the Stop flag set it should send or process no further DIOs for that graph and cancel any pending transmissions.

When the Target receives a P2P mode DIO, it finds inside it a complete source route from the Origin to itself. If the Origin asked for replies, the Target selects a route and sends it back in a reply message, one route per message. The Origin stores the discovered route in its memory. The Target may ask for an acknowledgement, and if none arrives within the P2P_DRO_ACK_WAIT_TIME interval it resends the reply, up to a certain number of times.
sections.plainLanguage: The temporary tree is only a place to build the route; it never carries data. When the target has what it needs it sends the route back, and if the reply is lost it sends it again.

sections.title: Interoperability with Core RPL
sections.content:
The memo describes how routers that implement P2P-RPL interact with routers that do not. In general, P2P-RPL operation does not affect core RPL operation and the other way round. There is one wrinkle: core RPL allows a router to join a DAG as a leaf node even if it does not understand the mode of operation used in that DAG, so a router without P2P-RPL may join a temporary graph and keep its membership even after the graph no longer exists. That may impose a drain on the router's memory.

Such routers do not interfere with the discovery itself, because a leaf node may only generate a DIO advertising an infinite rank, and every router implementing P2P-RPL is required to discard those. Core RPL also does not require a router to join a DAG whose mode of operation it does not understand, and a deployment may have strict restrictions on which graphs its routers may join, which mitigates the problem.

The mechanism works best when all the routers in the network implement P2P-RPL. In general, the ability to discover routes, and the quality of the routes discovered, deteriorate with the fraction of routers that do implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that does not know about this mechanism can still join the temporary tree and sit there wasting a little memory, but it does not get in the way of the discovery.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for P2P-RPL are broadly those for RPL. RPL's security framework provides data confidentiality, authentication, replay protection and delay protection, and it can be used in P2P-RPL once the constraints in the document are taken into account. All the routers taking part in a secure route discovery must use the security configuration chosen by the Origin, so that one weak router cannot compromise the whole discovery. A rogue router that tries a different configuration will, in the worst case, cause the discovery to fail, and in the best case cause its neighbours to act as firewalls and let the discovery proceed in the rest of the network.

The document makes one simplification. RPL describes three modes of security: unsecured, preinstalled and authenticated. Because a temporary graph is never used for routing packets, it is not meaningful to say that a node joins it as a router or a host, so in P2P-RPL there is no distinction between the preinstalled and authenticated modes. A router can join only if it can support the configuration in use, whether the key is preinstalled or dynamically acquired.

A rogue router that knows the key can still join and cause damage, by advertising false information, by sending bogus replies or by modifying genuine ones, and a rogue router acting as the Origin could launch denial-of-service attacks by starting fake discoveries. Because a reply travels along a source route named inside it, the concerns that led to the deprecation of Type 0 routing headers may apply, so each intermediate router must confirm that the route does not contain a loop involving itself before forwarding the message further.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router in the discovery has to use the security the Origin asked for, so a single weak router cannot weaken the whole thing. A router that knows the key can still lie, and the protocol checks the route for loops as the reply travels back.
